name: Guardian cryptic crossword, Penguin book 5 No 3

book.title: The New Penguin Book of The Guardian Crosswords, volume 5

entries.clue: Persian emperor’s rewritten chapter on coke (7,6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a possessive with its noun left out: what is the Persian emperor's, and what the answer names, is the seat he sits on.

indicatorNotes.rewritten: A chapter that has been rewritten holds the same material in a new arrangement, which is what happens to the letters standing after it.

blocks.note: thirteen letters to be set down in another order, which is the length the grid wants

annotation.surface: An emperor has gone back over the chapter he wrote about coke.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coke' reads as the drug or the drink and is four of the thirteen letters. The throne was the Mughal emperors' jewelled seat, carried off to Persia in 1739 and a byword for the Iranian monarchy ever since.
annotation.definitionFit: The Peacock Throne is the seat of the Persian shahs, so the thing that is the Persian emperor's, and the byword for his rule, is this.

entries.clue: Considers points for two lots of wise men? (9)

blocks.note: east and north are two of the compass points, and it is their initials that are wanted
wise men arrive three at a time, so two lots of them make six, and six in Roman figures is VI
a sage is a wise man, and the plural follows the plural in the clue

annotation.surface: Somebody is working out the points to award two parties of wise men.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Points' looks like a score being handed out and is the compass. The wise men who come in threes are the Magi of the Christmas story, which is the sum the question mark is covering.
annotation.definitionFit: To envisage a plan is to form a picture of it and turn it over, which is what it is to consider one.

entries.clue: Bring converse of train to road shortly (5)

indicatorNotes.converse of: The converse of a relation is the same pair taken the other way round, so the two means of transport named after it are written in the opposite order to the one the clue gives them in.
indicatorNotes.shortly: Shortly asks for the short form of a word rather than the whole of it, the version a map or a timetable prints.

blocks.note: the road's own vehicle, the one set against the train in any argument about transport
a train runs on a railway, which maps and timetables print as Ry

annotation.surface: The opposite of a train is due to reach the road before long.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Converse' is the logician's word: the converse of 'A to B' is 'B to A', which is what turns the two means of transport round. The proverb 15 is built on hangs on this verb.
annotation.definitionFit: To carry a thing is to convey it from one place to another on your person, which is what bringing it amounts to.

entries.clue: Carbon also used for burning (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition names the things by the job they do rather than by a synonym: the answer is a plural noun and burning is what these are kept for.

indicatorNotes.used: A thing that has been used comes back altered, so the letters standing beside it need not keep the order they were given; it is a gentle way of asking.

blocks.note: C is carbon's symbol on the periodic table
four letters re-set to follow the symbol

annotation.surface: Carbon is another of the things people burn.
annotation.walkthrough: Coal is mostly carbon, so the opening word belongs to the chemistry of the answer as well as to its letters. The definition says what the things are for and never names them.
annotation.definitionFit: Coals are the lumps of fuel kept by a grate, so their whole purpose is burning, which is what the definition points at.

entries.clue: Mock exam: what’s litmus? (4-5)

blocks.note: read as a school's practice run, printed and handed out a term before the real thing
read again as chemistry: the dye that goes red in acid and blue in alkali, sold soaked into little strips for dipping

annotation.surface: In the middle of a practice exam somebody asks what litmus actually is.
annotation.walkthrough: Both senses are paper that something is done with: one is printed with questions, the other steeped in dye. The hyphen in the enumeration is the only sign that two words are wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: A test paper is the sheet of questions a mock exam consists of, and litmus paper is the chemist's strip for testing acidity: the same two words in two trades.

entries.clue: Pretty girl goes bottom first into circle, refusing to comply (9)

indicatorNotes.goes bottom first: Going bottom first sends whatever is at the bottom round to the front, and in a down entry the bottom of a word is its last letter.
indicatorNotes.into: Going into something is going inside it, so what has just been rearranged is written within the word that follows.

blocks.note: a ring is a circle, and this one opens up to take the rest inside
a belle is a pretty girl, and the instruction beside her has already sent her last letter round to the front

annotation.surface: A pretty girl climbs into a circle bottom first and then will not do as she is told.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Belle' for a pretty girl is old-fashioned English borrowed from French. The clue depends on reading 'bottom' as a position rather than as a part of the girl, which is where the picture comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: To rebel is to refuse openly to obey whoever is in charge, and the -ing form matches 'refusing to comply' exactly.

entries.clue: Horse’s refusal, say? (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a possessive with its noun dropped — the horse's own noise — and the question mark is the licence the setter takes for it.

indicatorNotes.say: To say a thing is to make its sound, so what matters about the word in front is how it comes out of the mouth, not how it is spelt.

blocks.note: a refusal is a nay, the vote against a motion in its older spelling

annotation.surface: A horse refusing, at a fence perhaps.
annotation.walkthrough: A horse that stops dead at a fence is said to refuse, and the clue lets it announce the fact out loud. 'Nay' is the parliamentary no, the opposite of aye.
annotation.definitionFit: A neigh is the cry a horse makes, so the possessive with its noun left off points straight at the animal's own noise.

entries.clue: China Waller turns up with cars to rent (13)

indicatorNotes.turns up: What turns up is written the other way about, and in a down entry that means read from the foot of the column towards the top.

blocks.note: Fats Waller, the Harlem stride pianist of Ain't Misbehavin', with his first name set down as the instruction beside him asks
Ford is the make, so the plural is the cars themselves
to rent a car is to hire it

annotation.surface: A man called Waller arrives with cars he is offering for hire.
annotation.walkthrough: Fats Waller is the Waller meant, so it is his first name and not his surname that is turned. The Potteries — Stoke and its six towns — sit in this county, which is why its name will do for china.
annotation.definitionFit: A piece of Staffordshire is a piece of the china the county's potteries turned out, so the county's name stands for the ware itself.

entries.clue: Corn goddess keeps a lot of sticks on circle for measuring slow-down (13)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is the name of an instrument and the definition a phrase saying what it does; there is no one-word synonym, so the setter describes the job instead.

indicatorNotes.keeps: To keep a thing is to hold on to it, so the word in front opens up and everything else is written inside it.
indicatorNotes.a lot of: A lot of a word is most of it and not all, so what follows arrives one letter short at the end.
indicatorNotes.on: In a down entry whatever is on something else stands above it, so the sticks are written in first and the circle goes underneath them.

blocks.note: Demeter is the Greek goddess of the harvest, and she opens up to hold the rest
celery is sold in sticks, and the instruction in front stops the word short of its last letter
O is the round letter that stands for a circle

annotation.surface: The harvest goddess is hanging on to most of a bunch of sticks above a circle.
annotation.walkthrough: Ceres is the Roman name for the same goddess and would not have fitted; the clue wants the Greek one. A decelerometer is the gauge strapped into a vehicle to record how hard it brakes.
annotation.definitionFit: A decelerometer records how fast a moving thing is losing speed, which is exactly the slow-down the definition asks to have measured.

entries.clue: Acknowledgement about greeting to sailors in pub (Greek) (7)

indicatorNotes.about: What goes about a thing goes round it, so the word in front splits and stands on either side of everything that follows.

blocks.note: ta is the everyday British thank-you, and it parts to take the rest between its two letters
ave is the Latin hail, the greeting Romans wrote and Catholics still sing
the Royal Navy shortens to RN, and its men are the sailors meant

annotation.surface: A word of thanks and a greeting to the sailors drinking in a Greek bar.
annotation.walkthrough: The bracket is the setter naming a language rather than translating anything. 'Acknowledgement' is the thank-you sense, not a receipt, and it is the smallest of the three pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A taverna is the Greek version of the local, a small restaurant and bar, which is what the bracketed language is there to pin down.

entries.clue: Ottoman emperor’s vehicle returned with two drinks (English) (7,5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a possessive with its noun left out: the answer names the sultan's court and government, the institution that was his.

indicatorNotes.returned: What has returned has come back along the way it went, so the word in front is written from its far end; in an across entry that is right to left.

blocks.note: a bus is a vehicle, and the instruction beside it asks for those three letters the other way round
lime cordial is the first of the pair, the green squash of a pub counter
port, the fortified wine, is the second of the pair
E is the standard short form of English

annotation.surface: An emperor's vehicle comes back, and two drinks are ordered.
annotation.walkthrough: The Sublime Porte was the great gate of the sultan's palace in Constantinople where his ministers gave judgement, and then the name Europe used for the whole Ottoman government. The drinks belong to the pub, not the palace.
annotation.definitionFit: The Sublime Porte was the Ottoman sultan's court and administration, named for the gate it sat behind, so it is the thing that was the emperor's.

entries.clue: Suspicious, if perhaps reserved (5)

indicatorNotes.perhaps: 'Perhaps' allows the letters in front of it to stand in some order other than the one given, and where there are only two of them there is only one other order; it is a loose way of asking.

blocks.note: the two letters change places, which is the whole of what two letters can do
a reserved person is a shy one

annotation.surface: Something looks suspicious if it has perhaps been held back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reserved' is the pivot: the surface wants a table booked or a seat kept, and the wordplay wants the adjective for somebody quiet in company.
annotation.definitionFit: Something fishy smells wrong — a story or an alibi that invites doubt — so 'suspicious' is the plain adjective for it.

entries.clue: See about a lot of beauty in tomb (9)

indicatorNotes.about: What is about a thing is wrapped round it, so the word in front splits and the rest is set between its halves.
indicatorNotes.a lot of: A lot of a word is most of it and not the whole, so what follows arrives with its tail cut off.

blocks.note: the clue's own word taken at face value, opened up to hold what comes next
pulchritude is the formal word for beauty, and the instruction in front keeps most of it

annotation.surface: Somebody is being shown a good deal of the beauty inside a tomb.
annotation.walkthrough: Pulchritude is a Latinate word for good looks that survives mainly in jokes and crosswords, and it does all the work here. The Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem is the tomb the answer is best known for.
annotation.definitionFit: A sepulchre is a tomb cut in rock or built of stone, the word the Bible uses for the one Christ was laid in.

entries.clue: Paper instrument for a body (5)

blocks.note: read as newsprint: the journal a party or a union puts out to speak for it
read again as anatomy: the Greek word behind it means a tool, and a body's working parts are its tools

annotation.surface: An instrument made of paper, supplied to a body of some kind.
annotation.walkthrough: Three senses sit in five words: the party's journal, the pipes in the church loft, and the liver or the lungs. Only two of them are being defined, and the church is there for the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A party's paper is called its organ, the thing it speaks through; and an organ of a body is one of its instruments, from the Greek word for tool.

entries.clue: Where you needn’t 3 4 sounds 11 in 8 (9,5,4)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a cross-reference rather than a synonym: 8's answer is the county the place stands in, which is the clue's way of saying which of the two Newcastles is wanted.

indicatorNotes.sounds: 'Sounds' asks for what a word comes out as when it is spoken rather than how it is spelt, so the piece after it is written the way the ear takes it.

blocks.note: 3 and 4 spell out the errand of the proverb: taking coal to the town that dug it is the byword for a pointless journey
11's answer is the word said aloud here, and sub is Latin for under

annotation.walkthrough: Coals to Newcastle is the proverb for a wasted errand, and its Newcastle is the one on the Tyne; the joke is that this is the other one, a market town in the Potteries. Lyme was the forest it stood under.
annotation.definitionFit: Newcastle-under-Lyme is a Staffordshire town, so the county 8 spells out is what the clue offers in place of a definition, fixing which Newcastle to write.

entries.clue: Large size of dial put me off (9)

indicatorNotes.off: Something that has gone off is no longer as it should be, so the letters standing in front of it are not in the order they should be either.

blocks.note: nine letters to be set down in another order, which is the length the grid wants

annotation.surface: The sheer size of the dial was enough to put me off.
annotation.walkthrough: The three words that sound like a complaint about the dial are the material the clue works on. Physics borrowed the answer later for the height of a wave above its resting line.
annotation.definitionFit: Amplitude is the noun for being ample — roominess, generous extent — so 'large size' is its plain meaning underneath the scientific one.

entries.clue: She writes for the Thunderer and uses a disguise outside (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is a noun and the definition a clause: the setter says what she does instead of naming her, and 'she' is what makes the noun a feminine one.

indicatorNotes.disguise: A disguise leaves a thing recognisable but not as itself, so the letters it is put on come out in a different arrangement.
indicatorNotes.outside: What is outside stands round the rest, so those letters part and go on either side of what they are put outside of.

blocks.note: five letters re-set, and they part to stand on either side of the god
Thor is the Norse god of thunder, which his hammer makes

annotation.surface: A woman who writes for The Times and goes about in disguise.
annotation.walkthrough: The Thunderer is Fleet Street's old nickname for The Times, which is what the surface points at; the wordplay wants the god who actually makes the thunder.
annotation.definitionFit: An authoress is a woman who writes books, a feminine form now largely retired, so 'she writes' is the whole of it.

entries.clue: See 15
Washing-up liquid isn’t fit to drink (9)

annotation.definition: Washing-up liquid isn’t fit to drink

blocks.note: read as the bottle of detergent standing by the sink, and meant as the liquid you are left with once the plates are done
grey, greasy and going cold in the bowl — and the byword for tea that has been made far too weak

annotation.surface: A warning that the stuff in the bottle by the sink is not for drinking.
annotation.walkthrough: The trap is that washing-up liquid names a product in every British kitchen. The clue means its three words literally, and what they describe is the bowlful, not the bottle.
annotation.definitionFit: Dishwater is what stands in the bowl when the washing-up is over, and its name is proverbial for anything too weak and greasy to swallow.

entries.clue: Go without commercials? You surprise me! (5)

indicatorNotes.without: 'Without' in its older sense means outside, so the word in front stands round what follows instead of losing it.

blocks.note: the clue's own word, parted so that it stands on either side of the rest
the commercials between television programmes are ads

annotation.surface: Watching something that carries no advertisements at all.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Without' is the old preposition, the one in the hymn's green hill far away without a city wall: outside, not lacking. Gadso is a seventeenth-century oath, a politer stand-in for something stronger.
annotation.definitionFit: Gadso is an old exclamation of surprise or vexation, a softened oath, so it is what a speaker of the day said where we would say 'you surprise me!'

entries.clue: Prince on river with fool has some bread (4,1,4)

blocks.note: Prince Hal is Shakespeare's young Henry V, drinking his way through the taverns before he takes the crown
the Fal is the Cornish river that Falmouth stands at the mouth of
an oaf is a lumbering fool

annotation.surface: A prince beside a river with a fool, and some bread between them.
annotation.walkthrough: A prince and a fool in the same sentence is the Falstaff picture, which is what holds the surface together. Half a loaf is better than no bread is the proverb standing behind the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Half a loaf is literally part of a loaf — some bread rather than none — and the phrase lives on in the proverb about settling for it.

entries.clue: Queen of Californian city’s not broad in the beam (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer instead of naming it: the thing is a beam, and what the clue says about it is that it is a very narrow one.

indicatorNotes.of: 'Queen of the city's' is the double genitive of ordinary speech — the city's queen — so the city and its apostrophe-s are written first and the queen comes after.

blocks.note: Los Angeles shortens to LA, and the clue's own apostrophe-s follows it
ER is the Queen's cipher, Elizabeth Regina, stamped on British post boxes

annotation.surface: A beauty queen from a Californian city who is not wide across the hips.
annotation.walkthrough: Broad in the beam is a ship's width carried over to a person's hips, and the answer is a beam of quite another kind. Los Angeles is the Californian city every crossword means.
annotation.definitionFit: A laser is a beam of light so narrow it stays a pencil over miles, which is what 'not broad in the beam' is claiming of it.

entries.clue: French for good could be scarlet (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition does not name a kind of scarlet: it points at the pair of words the answer completes, the childhood illness whose rash supplies the colour.

blocks.note: F is the standard short form of French
what has gone for good has gone for ever, and it is the second word of that phrase that is wanted

annotation.surface: The French word for 'good' might turn out to be a shade of red.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface offers 'the French for good', as though a translation were being asked for, and the clue means its two halves separately. Scarlet fever takes its name from the rash that comes with it.
annotation.definitionFit: Scarlet fever is the childhood illness the colour word belongs to, so what 'scarlet' turns out to be short for is the answer.

entries.clue: See 11
Fear makes father less than agreeable (5)

indicatorNotes.less than: Less than the whole of something is that thing cut short, so the word after it gives up its ending.

blocks.note: pa is the nursery word for father
nice is agreeable, and the instruction in front takes the last letter off it

annotation.surface: Fear is turning a father into somebody less than pleasant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Less than agreeable' is the polite British way of calling somebody unpleasant, which is why it reads as comment rather than instruction. The word itself comes from the god Pan and the terror he spread through lonely places.
annotation.definitionFit: Panic is fear at its most sudden and least reasoning, the kind that empties a building, so 'fear' is the plain noun for it.

entries.clue: Badge put in parrot fashion (7)

indicatorNotes.in: What is put in something goes inside it, so the word before it is written between the halves of the words after it.

blocks.note: learning something parrot fashion is learning it by rote, and those four letters part to take the rest inside
to put a thing down is to set it down

annotation.surface: A badge pinned on in the manner of a parrot.
annotation.walkthrough: Parrot fashion is how a child learns a times table: by repetition, with no understanding of it at all. The badge is the ribbon a candidate wears at an election count.
annotation.definitionFit: A rosette is the ribbon badge pinned on at an election or a horse show, which is the sense of badge the clue wants.

entries.clue: Brown beard in front trench (7)

annotation.definitionNote: Two senses stand side by side rather than one: Vandyke brown is a pigment and a Vandyke is a beard, so the definition is not describing a beard that happens to be brown.

blocks.note: the van is the front — the vanguard of an army is its leading part
a dyke is a ditch cut into the ground, the trench that drains a field

annotation.surface: A brown beard seen in the front trench.
annotation.walkthrough: Anthony Van Dyck painted Charles I and his court wearing the neat pointed beard that took his name, and the dark brown of those canvases took it too. The trenches are the surface's own idea.
annotation.definitionFit: Vandyke brown is the dark pigment named after the painter, and a Vandyke is the trim pointed beard he gave his sitters: two separate senses of one word.

entries.clue: Smile about ruse in changing fees? I’m too sad to (5-8)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a sentence broken off: too sad to smile, with the missing verb supplied by the clue's own first word, and the answer is the adjective for the person saying it.

indicatorNotes.about: What goes about a thing is wrapped round it, so the word in front splits and everything else is written between its halves.
indicatorNotes.in: What is in something sits inside it, so the word before it is written within the letters that follow.
indicatorNotes.changing: Fees that are changing are not staying as they were, so the four letters beside the word are set down in a new order.

blocks.note: a grin is a smile, and it opens up to hold everything else
four letters re-set, and they part in turn to make room for the ruse
a ruse is a trick

annotation.surface: Somebody cannot manage a smile about a scam involving altered fees.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition needs the clue's first word to finish it: too sad to smile. 'Changing fees' is the sort of thing a bank announces, which is what makes the whole sentence sound like a complaint.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody grief-stricken has been struck down by grief and is in no state to smile, which is exactly what the broken-off sentence says of itself.
